claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr has inherent atomic-scale chemical disorder.
The as-synthesized HfNbTaTiZr specimen contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Variations in atomic masses and local force constants are characteristic sources of disorder in high-entropy alloys.
Local lattice distortions are intrinsic to solid-solution alloys with differing atomic radii.
Lattice-distortion and defect-scattering metrics are relevant to thermal transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Thermal conductivity can be separated into lattice and electronic contributions.
An ML framework using atomistic disorder and oxygen-contamination descriptors can independently predict lattice and electronic thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
Nonlinear regression over simulation-derived data can identify and decouple the phononic and electronic transport channels in this alloy.
Refined phonon spectra and Boltzmann transport calculations provide suitable high-fidelity inputs for the proposed model.
Below 200 K, the lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions of HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
From 300 to 1200 K, HfNbTaTiZr has low total thermal conductivity that is affected by minor oxygen contamination.
Conventional Debye- or DFT-based models generally assume defect-free crystals.
Conventional models typically conflate lattice and electronic thermal transport.
The proposed model will improve predictive accuracy by approximately 15–20% relative to conventional models.
Separate lattice and electronic conductivity predictions will each agree with experimental measurements within ±15–20%.
The model is applicable to low-oxygen HfNbTaTiZr below 200 K and from 300 to 1200 K.

Inelastic neutron scattering or Raman spectroscopy can independently determine lattice thermal conductivity, while terahertz spectroscopy or Hall measurements can independently determine electronic thermal conductivity.
An error greater than ±15–20% for either separated contribution in either temperature regime would falsify the hypothesis.
